newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. activist Wu says HK handover a "tragedy".
newsitem.headline: U.S. activist Wu says HK handover a "tragedy".

text.p: Chinese-American human rights activist Harry Wu, who paid a secret visit to Hong Kong last week, told a local newspaper the territory's handover to China on July 1 was a "tragedy".

"I think the handover is a tragedy," Wu told the Sunday edition of the Hong Kong Standard, adding he was not sure whether he would be allowed to return to the territory after China takes it back from Britain at midnight on June 30.
"Hong Kong will become part of China and they hate me in China," said Wu, who now lives in San Francisco as a U.S. citizen.

Shanghai-born Wu, who spent 19 years in forced labour camps in China in the 1960s and 1970s, visited Hong Kong last week with a French television crew filming a documentary about the handover and stayed at a hotel under a false name, the paper said.

Wu told Reuters in the United States last week he was certain Beijing would introduce repressive measures into the territory of 6.4 million people, despite China's pledge to allow Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy after the handover.
"Hong Kong is finished," he told Reuters. "Do you think a free capitalist system under totalitarianism can survive?"

China has already alarmed many people inside and outside the territory by proposing to repeal some Hong Kong legislation enshrining civil rights -- ordinances it has said were not consistent with the territory's post-handover constitution.
China also plans to replace the elected legislature with a hand-picked provisional body.
Beijing would not overtly crack down on mainland dissidents living in Hong Kong after the handover, Wu told the Standard, because it wanted to give the impression of a smooth changeover.
"Keeping things in low profile includes dealing with Hong Kong dissident organisations, religious groups and so on," he said.
"The Chinese government won't arrest them -- that would be stupid. But that doesn't mean not doing anything."
